extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics and creative writers of epic/tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic and tragic poetry (unity, plot-types, diction, metre, handling of the marvellous, error/objection responses), based on Aristotle's Poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of epic (simple/complex; character vs calamity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be the same varieties of epic as of tragedy: an epic must be 'simple' or 'complex,' or else turn on 'character' or on 'calamity.' The constituent parts, too, are the same with the exception of song and spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic should employ reversals, discoveries, and calamities; thought and diction must be good. Examples: the Iliad as a 'simple' story turning on calamity; the Odyssey as 'complex' and full of discoveries, turning on character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and unity (beginning to end graspable)
rubrics_metrics.description: The limit of length ... will suffice — it must be possible to embrace the beginning and the end in one view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compositions should be short enough that beginning and end are apprehended together (roughly comparable to the length of tragedies presented at a single entertainment). Epic has an advantage in being narrative (can portray simultaneous incidents) which, if relevant, increases variety and richness; avoid monotony that satiates the audience. If an epic takes multiple separate actions it reduces unity and risks seeming dilute or curtailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate metre (heroic hexameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience has shown that the heroic hexameter is the right metre. Were anyone to write a narrative poem in any other metre or in several metres, the effect would be wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hexameter is sedate and dignified and permits rare words and metaphors. Iambic and trochaic tetrameters suit lively/dancing or 'real life' effects. Do not mix several metres in a long narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic representation / persona (avoid authorial intrusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as seldom as possible in his own character, since he is not 'representing' the story in that sense. Homer brings in persons who 'have character of their own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer assuming a character and representing through character rather than continual authorial commentary or playing a part throughout the poem. Excessive authorial presence weakens representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the marvellous and the inexplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The marvellous should certainly be portrayed in tragedy, but epic affords greater scope for the inexplicable (which is the chief element in what is marvellous), because we do not actually see the persons of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is convincing though impossible should always be preferred to what is possible and unconvincing. Inexplicable elements should, as far as possible, be avoided in the play itself and, if present, should lie outside the story (e.g., Oedipus not knowing how Laius died). Use of the marvellous must not impair plausibility for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: restraint and place for elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated only in the 'idle' parts which do not reveal character or thought. Too brilliant diction frustrates its own object by diverting attention from the portrayal of character and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve highly elaborate or dazzling language for passages that do not require revelation of character or core thought. Excessive brilliance in key moments distracts and weakens dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of poetic error (essential vs accidental)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the actual art of poetry there are two kinds of errors, essential and accidental. If a man meant to represent something and failed through incapacity, that is an essential error. But if his error is due to his original conception being wrong that is accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish errors in poetic art from technical or factual errors in special branches of knowledge; an impossibility portrayed may be acceptable if it achieves the poetic object, but if the same effect could be achieved without sacrificing technical accuracy, the error is culpable. Example: Hector's pursuit may be an intolerable absurdity on stage but acceptable in epic narration if it achieves effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible defenses for improbability or impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Any 'impossibility' may be defended by reference to the poetic effect or to the ideal or to current opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible defenses include: (a) the poetic effect (a convincing impossibility preferred), (b) representation of people 'as they ought to be' (ideal), (c) appeal to popular tradition or current belief, (d) historical/unfamiliar customs. If improbability is unnecessary and unused, censure is due (examples: gratuitous introductions like Aegeus in Medea; immoral characterization without necessity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for meeting critical objections (the twelve heads)
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticizing expressions we should consider a dozen grounds of explanation: things as they were; things as they are; things as they are said and seem to be; things as they should be; and also linguistic/interpretive factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit list to consult when resolving objections: (1) things as they were; (2) things as they are; (3) things as they are said to be; (4) things as they seem to be; (5) things as they ought to be; (6) a rare word; (7) a metaphor; (8) the right accent; (9) punctuation; (10) ambiguity; (11) habitual use of the phrase; (12) the proper standard of correctness in poetry as distinct from other arts. Use these to re-interpret problematic passages (examples given from Homer, Empedocles, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of censure against a poet
rubrics_metrics.description: The censures they bring are of five kinds: that things are either impossible or irrational or harmful or inconsistent or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study alleged faults under these five heads and then apply the twelve interpretive remedies/considerations to assess whether the censure holds or is answerable by poetic conventions, diction, metaphor, popular tradition, or necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative plausibility techniques (use of convincing fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer has taught the others the proper way of telling lies, that is, by using a fallacy: When B is true if A is true, people think that if B is true A must be true or happen. Therefore if A be untrue and B is necessarily true if A is true, the proper thing to do is to posit B...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ tightly convincing consequences or plausible particulars (even if logically linked to a false antecedent) so that audience inference accepts the antecedent; prefer convincing impossibility to unconvincing possibility. Use this technique sparingly and ethically for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of inexplicable elements (inside vs outside the story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should not be made up of inexplicable details; so far as possible there should be nothing inexplicable, or, if there is, it should lie outside the story — as, for instance, Oedipus not knowing how Laius died — and not in the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an inexplicable fact is essential, place it so that it does not contradict onstage logic or degrade dramatic plausibility; do not construct a plot primarily by means of inexplicable contrivances when a more reasonable treatment is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative merits of tragedy versus epic (unity, economy, spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has all the elements of the epic and in addition a considerable element of its own in the spectacle and the music, which make the pleasure all the more vivid; and it attains its end with greater economy of length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate form by: (a) the economy and concentration of effect (concentrated art is more effective than spread-out epic treatment), (b) vividness added by spectacle and music (which operate whether read or acted), (c) unity — tragedy's concentrated single action often achieves greater unity than epic, which can be composed of several separate actions. Note: shortcomings of acting (vulgarity, overacting) are defects of performance not of the tragic art itself.
